primer.intro: A hash map buys you one superpower: have I seen this before, answered in constant time. This topic spends that superpower on subarray questions that look quadratic. The key move is the prefix trick: let prefix(i) be the sum of everything up to index i; then a subarray from j+1 to i sums to k exactly when prefix(i) minus prefix(j) equals k - so instead of scanning all subarrays, walk once and ask the map whether prefix(i) minus k has appeared. The same identity works with XOR in place of sum, because XOR is its own inverse. And for the longest run of consecutive values, a hash set answers the only question that matters: is this number the start of a run?
whenToUse: Counting subarrays with a given sum or XOR - prefix values plus a frequency map.
Longest subarray with a given sum when negatives exist - first-seen prefix indexes.
Longest streak of consecutive values in any order - a set plus a start-of-run test.
Any pairing question shaped like a plus b equals target - store complements as you walk.
primer.mentalModel: Think of prefixes as mile markers along the array. Every subarray is the gap between two markers, so a question about subarrays becomes a question about pairs of markers - and pairing questions are what hash maps eat. Counting: keep how many times each prefix value has occurred; at marker p, every earlier marker worth p minus k closes one valid subarray, so add that count. Longest: keep the first index where each prefix value occurred; p minus k seen earliest gives the widest gap. One seed makes it honest: the empty prefix 0 exists before the array starts - map it to count 1 or index -1 - or every subarray that begins at index 0 goes missing. For consecutive streaks, dump everything in a set and walk up only from numbers whose predecessor is absent: each run is then walked exactly once.
mistakes: Forgetting to seed the empty prefix (0 maps to count 1, index -1) - subarrays starting at index 0 vanish.
Using the sliding window on sum questions with negatives - the window logic assumes growth; prefixes do not.
Walking up from every member of the set instead of only run-starts - the streak scan turns quadratic.

example.title: Counting subarrays that sum to k
example.explain: At each element the running prefix asks one question: how many earlier prefixes equal prefix minus k? Each of those marks a starting point whose subarray ends here with sum exactly k, so the stored frequency is added wholesale. The seed seen(0) = 1 represents the empty prefix before the array, which is what lets a subarray starting at index 0 close. Swap plus for XOR and the lookup to prefix XOR k, and the identical loop counts XOR-k subarrays.

primer.practice: Open Practice with Longest Consecutive Sequence for the set trick, then Count Subarrays with Given Sum to engrave the prefix-map loop.

sections.title: Prefix sums meet maps
sections.text: The identity to memorise: sum of a subarray ending at i and starting after j is prefix(i) minus prefix(j). Fix the right end at i and the question - does some subarray ending here sum to k - becomes: has prefix(i) minus k occurred as an earlier marker? A map answers in constant time, and what you store in it decides the problem solved. Store counts and you count subarrays. Store first indexes and you maximise length - longest subarray with sum k, or with sum 0 as the special case k equals 0. Store last indexes and you would minimise instead. XOR obeys the same algebra since x XOR x cancels: prefix-XOR markers, lookup prefix XOR k, same loop, same seed, same bill of one pass.

check.prompt: Array 1 1 1, k = 2, map seeded with prefix 0 count 1. How many subarrays sum to 2?

options.explain: Prefixes 1, 2, 3: at 2 the map holds one 0; at 3 it holds one 1 - two closures.
Both (1,1) windows count: positions 0-1 and 1-2.
Three would need a third prefix pair differing by 2 - there are two.
The seed plus prefix 2 closes a subarray immediately.

reveal.solution: Walk it. Prefixes run 1, 2, 3. At prefix 1: lookup 1 - 2 = -1, absent, count 0. At prefix 2: lookup 0, present once (the seed) - count 1; that is the subarray 0..1. At prefix 3: lookup 1, present once - count 2; that is the subarray 1..2. The seed is what let the first closure happen: it stands for the empty prefix before index 0.

sections.title: Sets that spot starts
sections.text: Longest consecutive sequence looks like a sorting problem and is secretly a membership problem. Pour the array into a hash set - duplicates collapse free of charge - then walk the set and ask one filtering question per value: is value minus 1 absent? Only then is this value the start of a run, and only then do you count upward: value plus 1, plus 2, onward while membership holds. Every run is traversed exactly once from its true start, so the total work stays linear even though a while loop sits inside a for loop. Skip the filter and a single long run gets rewalked from every one of its members - the classic quadratic accident this problem exists to teach.

quiz.prompt: Longest streak of consecutive values, array in any order. The linear plan?

options.text: Two nested loops hunting value + 1
options.explain: Quadratic - every member searches the whole array.

options.text: A set; walk up only from values whose predecessor is absent
options.explain: Each run is counted once, from its true start - linear total.

options.text: Sort, then scan for runs
options.explain: Correct, but n log n - the set answers membership without ordering.

options.text: A prefix-sum array over the values
options.explain: Prefix sums answer subarray-sum questions; streaks are about membership of neighbouring values.

quiz.prompt: Longest subarray with sum k when the array holds negatives. The tool?

options.text: Sort the array first
options.explain: Subarrays live in the original order; sorting destroys them.

options.text: Try every start and end
options.explain: The quadratic baseline the prefix map replaces.

options.text: First-seen index per prefix sum; at p, the earliest p - k gives the widest gap
options.explain: First occurrence maximises length; negatives are no obstacle to prefixes.

options.text: A sliding window that shrinks when the sum passes k
options.explain: Shrinking assumes adding elements grows the sum - negatives break that.

quiz.prompt: Count subarrays with sum exactly k. What does the map store?

options.text: How many times each prefix value occurred; add the count of prefix - k
options.explain: Every stored occurrence closes one subarray ending here.

options.text: The first index of each prefix value
options.explain: First-index maps answer longest, counting needs frequencies.

options.text: The elements themselves
options.explain: Membership of elements cannot see subarray sums.

options.text: Running maximums per index
options.explain: Maximums belong to other problems; sums need prefix markers.

quiz.prompt: Count subarrays whose XOR equals k. Why does the prefix trick survive the swap?

options.text: XOR is its own inverse, so segment XOR is prefix XOR prefix - lookup prefix XOR k
options.explain: x XOR x cancels, exactly like subtraction cancels addition.

options.text: XOR is commutative
options.explain: Commutativity helps, but self-inverse is what isolates the segment.

options.text: It only works when k is 0
options.explain: Any k works; the lookup key just becomes prefix XOR k.

options.text: It does not - XOR needs nesting loops
options.explain: The identical one-pass loop counts XOR subarrays.

quiz.prompt: Array 1 1 1, k = 2. How many subarrays sum to 2?

options.explain: The two windows overlap but count separately.
Two adjacent ones make 2 twice over.
Positions 0-1 and 1-2 - the prefix walk closes once at 2, once at 3.
The whole array sums to 3, one too many.
Both runs are longer than a pair.
100-102 is a run of three; the ones digit run goes one longer.
Seven needs every value consecutive - 4 and 100 break it.

quiz.prompt: Array 9 -3 3 -1 6 -5. Length of the largest zero-sum subarray?

options.explain: Repeated prefix value 9 proves a zero-sum stretch exists.
-3 + 3 - 1 + 6 - 5 = 0: prefix 9 reappears at the end, gap of five.
-3, 3 is a zero pair, but the five-wide stretch also cancels.
The whole array sums to 9, no cancel.

quiz.prompt: The prefix-map counting loop over n elements costs how much?

options.text: Quadratic time
options.explain: Quadratic is the all-subarrays baseline the map removes.

options.text: n log n
options.explain: No sorting happens; hash operations skip the log.

options.text: Linear time, constant space
options.explain: The map can hold n distinct prefixes - space is the price paid.

options.text: Linear time, linear space - one pass, one map entry per prefix
options.explain: Each element does one lookup and one insert at constant expected cost.

quiz.prompt: Longest consecutive: sorting solves it in n log n. What does the set version pay?

options.text: Also n log n
options.explain: Hash sets skip ordering entirely; no log remains.

options.text: Quadratic
options.explain: Quadratic happens only when the start filter is forgotten.

options.text: Constant
options.explain: Every element must at least be inserted - linear is the floor.

options.text: Expected linear - each run is walked once from its start
options.explain: The predecessor filter guarantees one traversal per run.

quiz.prompt: This streak finder times out on one long run of consecutive values. What is the bug?

options.text: len must start at 0
options.explain: Starting at 1 counts x itself, which is right.

options.text: Math.max is slow
options.explain: The rewalking dominates everything else.

options.text: No start filter - every member rewalks the run; skip x when x - 1 is in the set
options.explain: With the filter each run is traversed once; without it, quadratic.

options.text: The while should test x - len
options.explain: Walking downward has the same cost; direction is no cure.

quiz.prompt: This counter misses every subarray that starts at index 0. What is the bug?

options.text: prefix should reset when it exceeds k
options.explain: Prefixes never reset - the map remembers for them.

options.text: count needs Math.max instead of +=
options.explain: Counting accumulates; max would answer a different question.

options.text: The empty prefix is unseeded - start the map with 0 mapping to 1
options.explain: Subarrays from index 0 close against the empty prefix; seed it.

options.text: The insert must happen before the lookup
options.explain: That order would let a subarray of length zero count itself.

quiz.prompt: Which input most deserves a dedicated test for prefix-sum counting?

options.text: One whose only valid subarray starts at index 0
options.explain: It closes against the seeded empty prefix - the seed's whole job.

options.text: A strictly increasing array
options.explain: Pleasant prefixes, nothing boundary-shaped.

options.text: An array of one large value
options.explain: Fine as a smoke test; the index-0 closure finds the real bug.

options.text: k larger than the total sum
options.explain: Zero matches is an easy, honest answer.
